title: Can I Improve Egg Quality? What Does the Evidence Say?
seoTitle: Can you improve egg quality? What the evidence shows
description: No test measures egg quality directly, and no supplement is proven to fix it. Here is what age, habits and fertility tests can and cannot tell you.
directAnswer: Egg quality mostly means whether an egg carries the right number of chromosomes and can develop into a healthy embryo. Age is the strongest known influence, and no blood test or scan measures quality directly. Stopping smoking, keeping a healthy weight and limiting alcohol support general fertility, but no habit, supplement or package has been shown to reliably reverse age-related change in egg quality. A fertility clinician can explain what your own results mean.

sections.heading: What people mean by egg quality
paragraphs: Clinicians usually use egg quality to describe how likely an egg is to be chromosomally normal, fertilise, and grow into an embryo that can implant. As women get older, a larger share of eggs have chromosome errors. That shift explains much of the fall in monthly pregnancy chances and the rise in miscarriage risk with age.

Egg quantity is a separate idea. Ovarian reserve describes roughly how many eggs remain, and it also falls with age. Two people of the same age can have very different reserve, yet the chromosomal pattern of their eggs tends to follow age more closely than any reserve number.

This difference matters when you read advertising. A product that claims to “boost egg quality” is making a claim about chromosomes and embryo development, which is hard to prove and rarely tested in well-designed human trials.

sections.heading: What fertility tests can and cannot show
paragraphs: AMH blood tests and antral follicle counts on ultrasound estimate ovarian reserve. ASRM explains that these markers help predict how the ovaries may respond to stimulation medicines during IVF. They do not tell you whether an individual egg is healthy, and a low AMH does not on its own mean you cannot conceive naturally.

During IVF, embryologists can look at how eggs and embryos develop in the laboratory, and some clinics offer genetic testing of embryos. Even those observations are indirect, and they only become available once treatment has started. Our guide on what AMH can and cannot tell you covers the reserve test in more detail.

ASRM's guidance on fertility evaluation supports choosing tests based on your history and goals rather than ordering a fixed panel for everyone. Be cautious about clinics or apps that sell a single number as a measure of egg quality.

sections.heading: Habits that support fertility, and their limits
paragraphs: ASRM's patient material on optimising natural fertility points to a few practical areas. Smoking is linked to faster loss of eggs and earlier menopause, so stopping is one of the clearest steps. Very high or very low body weight can disturb ovulation. Heavy alcohol use and recreational drugs are worth stopping when trying to conceive, and moderate caffeine intake is generally considered acceptable.

These habits support overall reproductive health and a healthier pregnancy. What the evidence does not show is that any of them can turn back the age-related rise in chromosome errors. Framing lifestyle change as general preparation, not an egg-repair plan, avoids guilt if pregnancy takes longer than hoped.

If you are planning a pregnancy, our preconception planning checklist and fertility preparation guide cover folic acid, vaccinations, existing conditions and medicines. Folic acid is recommended to lower the risk of neural tube defects in the baby, not because it improves eggs.

sections.heading: Supplements, packages and 90-day promises
paragraphs: Supplements such as CoQ10, DHEA, myo-inositol, melatonin and antioxidant blends are widely marketed for egg quality. Human studies are mostly small, mixed in design and focused on IVF patients, and they have not shown a consistent improvement in live birth rates. Professional bodies do not recommend a routine supplement for egg quality.

Some products contain hormones or ingredients that interact with medicines, thyroid treatment or IVF protocols. Tell your fertility team about everything you take, including herbal and Ayurvedic preparations, so they can check whether it is safe for you.

Be wary of claims that eggs can be “reset” in 90 days, of fertility diets sold as cures, and of costly test-and-supplement bundles. Eggs do mature over a few months, but that timeline does not mean a product can change their chromosomes.

sections.heading: Questions to ask a fertility clinician
paragraphs: Useful questions include: What do my age, AMH and follicle count suggest about reserve and likely response to treatment? Is there anything in my history, such as endometriosis, previous ovarian surgery or smoking, that affects my eggs? How long should we try before testing or treatment, given my age?

You can also ask whether any supplement you are taking is worth continuing, what the evidence is for any add-on a clinic offers, and whether options such as egg freezing are relevant if pregnancy is not planned soon. Dr. Charmi Shah can review your results and talk through these choices with you.

sections.heading: When to seek help sooner
paragraphs: Seek a fertility assessment after a year of trying if you are under 35, after six months if you are 35 or over, and sooner if you have very irregular or absent periods, known endometriosis, previous pelvic infection or surgery, or a partner with known sperm problems.

During fertility treatment, severe abdominal pain, marked swelling, breathlessness or passing very little urine are reasons to be assessed in person. Our doctors arrange urgent hospital care for these only when your assessment shows it is clinically required. If you are already very unwell, do not wait for a reply on this website. Quieter concerns can be raised at a booked consultation.

faqs.question: Does a low AMH mean my eggs are poor quality?
faqs.answer: No. AMH reflects roughly how many eggs remain and how the ovaries may respond to IVF medicines. It does not measure whether individual eggs are chromosomally healthy, and age remains the main guide to egg quality.

faqs.question: Can supplements make my eggs younger?
faqs.answer: No supplement has been shown to reverse age-related change in egg quality. Some have small, mixed studies in IVF patients. Discuss any product with your fertility clinician before taking it, especially during treatment.

faqs.question: Is egg freezing a way to protect egg quality?
faqs.answer: Freezing eggs at a younger age preserves eggs as they are at that time. It does not ensure a future pregnancy, and success depends heavily on age at freezing and the number of eggs stored.

sourcesChecked.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve
sourcesChecked.recommendation: AMH and antral follicle count estimate reserve and predict stimulation response; they do not measure egg quality or reliably predict natural conception.
sourcesChecked.limitations: Reserve markers need interpretation with age and clinical context.

sourcesChecked.title: Optimizing natural fertility
sourcesChecked.recommendation: Avoid smoking, keep a healthy weight, limit alcohol, moderate caffeine; age is the major factor in fertility.
sourcesChecked.limitations: General associations do not prove that a specific change improves egg quality.
